claims.text: Temporal's default Activity retry policy has no attempt limit (maximumAttempts 0 is evaluated as unlimited), starting at a 1 second interval, doubling, and capping at 100 seconds.
Temporal's docs-derived advice is to set maximumAttempts on any Activity that costs money, such as a paid LLM call, because the default retry policy is unlimited.
Restate retries a ctx.run block or the whole invocation by default 70 times with backoff starting at 50 ms, doubling, up to 60 seconds, after which the invocation pauses.
Inngest retries each step.run() with its own counter; default is 5 attempts (first try plus 4 retries) with exponential backoff and jitter.
DBOS step retries are off by default; when turned on the default is 3 attempts with 1 second backoff doubling.
DBOS's @DBOS.step() decorator takes retriesAllowed, intervalSeconds, and maxAttempts, making retry policy per-step and declarative.
Inngest throws NonRetriableError for permanent failures and RetryAfterError to control retry timing; step.waitForEvent() returns null on timeout, and match and if cannot be combined.
DBOS has no selective non-retryable-exception support, so with step retries enabled a misconfigured agent burns its full retry budget before failing.

Pydantic AI docs warn Temporal's default RetryPolicy.maximum_attempts of 0 means unbounded re-execution of model requests, and recommend disabling the provider client's own retries (e.g. max_retries=0) to avoid retry multiplication.
With Restate and the Vercel AI SDK, each Restate invocation retry goes through the AI SDK's maxRetries attempts again (default 2), so the two retry layers multiply.
Every retry engine runs tool calls at least once, so the only reliable way to avoid a duplicated side effect is an idempotency key that the receiving API checks.

Temporal has no built-in dedup key; the recommended idempotency key is the Workflow Run ID plus the Activity ID. Restate uses an Idempotency-Key header (24 hours), Inngest an event id or idempotency expression (24 hours), DBOS the workflow ID.

In a Temporal example, the refund Activity receives an idempotency key built from `${workflowInfo().workflowId}:issue-refund`; the Inngest equivalent uses `${runId}:issue-refund`, and the DBOS version uses `{DBOS.workflow_id}:issue_refund`.
On a Temporal crash, completed activities are replayed from history, but the in-flight activity is restarted from the beginning, so a tool like issue_refund still needs an idempotency key.
Temporal recommends setting a Start-To-Close Timeout because the server does not detect failures when a Worker loses communication or crashes; the timeout is what forces Activity retries.
Temporal handles human-in-the-loop approvals via Signals and a durable condition wait (e.g. 7 days), during which no worker is held.
In Temporal, workflow.wait_condition is the durable suspend point for approvals; the workflow consumes no compute while waiting and resumes when the approve signal arrives.
Inngest's step.waitForEvent suspends a function awaiting an approval event (e.g. 'refund/approved' with a 3-day timeout, matched on ticketId) before high-impact actions like refunds.
Inngest states that a wait does not keep a worker running, and each completed step's result is stored as a checkpoint.

In a Martin Fowler article, measured waiting workflows used no CPU on either Cloudflare or local Temporal; a workflow in memory woke in 14 ms on Temporal, and one rebuilt from the log took under 0.1 s on Temporal versus about 2 s on Cloudflare.
Temporal's continue_as_new carries state into a fresh run with an empty history, which keeps replay fast for long-lived entity workflows such as one-per-SKU agents.
Temporal supports saga compensation for multi-tool agents: when a step fails beyond its retry limit, the workflow runs compensating activities in reverse order.
DBOS writes a workflow_status row as PENDING with inputs, stores each step output in an operation_outputs table, and on restart resumes PENDING workflows from the last completed step.
Temporal is reported as used in production by OpenAI for Codex, Stripe, Netflix, and Snap.
Inngest production users include Day.ai and Browser Use.
